newsitem.title: USA: AT&T in cost-cut plan, near-term earnings hurt.
newsitem.headline: AT&T in cost-cut plan, near-term earnings hurt.

text.p: AT&T Corp said its near-term earnings will be hurt by a series of actions that include cost-cutting moves and heavy investmemnts to allow it to enter new markets, including the local serivice business.

At the opening of a two-day meeting with analysts AT&T President John Walter said the company expected 1997 year earnings from core long distance and wireless businesses of $3.45 to $3.75 per share, compared to $3.47 reported in 1996.
In a drive to control costs, he said the company expected to make $2.6 billion in cuts over the next two years, a portion of which is reflected in the 1997 target earnings.
In addition, AT&T officials said first quarter 1996 earnings could be up to 10 percent below the $0.76 per share reported in last year's fourth quarter.
Walter said the company was committed to producing earnings of $5.00 to $6.00 per share within five years.

"We're committed to $5.00 to $6.00 per share of earnings in five years," Walter said. "As we aggressively operationalize our strategy and relentlessly focus on cost and execution, I am confident we will reach that target."
Prior to the announcement, the Wall Street consensus for the 1997 year was $3.40 per share, according to First Call.

"In the short-term, the investments will put increasing strain on our financial performance," AT&T Chairman Robert Allen said. "These investments put AT&T on a path for powerful growth, but there's no question that they will dilute earnings in the near term."
Allen also said AT&T is moving quickly to a market- and customer-focused organization from a product-focused one.

He said the move away from a product focus will allow it to meet customer demands for packages of services, including wireless, local and long distance, along with advanced information services and Internet-based electronic commerce.
AT&T's core long distance and traditional wireless services businesses in 1996 earned about $4.06 per share.

But 1996 earnings were diluted about $0.59 per share by spending on growth initiatives, including AT&T's entry into local and on-line services, international ventures, outsourcing and other factors, the company said.
As a result, AT&T's 1996 reported earnings were $3.47 per share.
Walter said the drop in core business earnings verus 1996 is largely due to greater depreciation costs as a result of significantly boosted capital spending in the past few years.

Other factors he cited included the higher cost of purchasing hardware and software at retail from the recently spun off Lucent Technologies, and the expected continuing competitive pressure on our consumer business.
He said AT&T's top priority is to create value for shareowners by "fixing our problems, strategically growing revenue, decisively cutting costs, delivering with speed and investing wisely."
He said AT&T is changing its management compensation structure to align rewards with shareowners' priorities.
"Compensation will be more directly tied to business performance metrics, with stock-ownership targets for senior management," he said.
Walter said plans were still under development for how the company would acheive the proposed $2.6 billion in cuts over the next two years.

The company said expenses associated with new growth initiatives could diminish AT&T's financial results from the core business by $0.75 to $1.00 per share in 1997 and are not reflected in the target core earnings range.

AT&T warned that if competitive pressures in the consumer business intensify -- or new competitors such as the Regional Bell companies enter during the year -- additional pressure will be put on earnings and the core range could be lower.

Walter said that despite complex technology, regulatory, financial and marketplace demands, the company fully intends to "unleash the power of AT&T and play offense" by continuing to invest in growth initiatives and the infrastructure necessary for the changing industry environment.
He estimated these investments would result in 1997 capital spending in the range of $8 to $9 billion.
-- New York newsdesk, 212-859-1610
